The West Eifel Volcanic Field of western Germany, SW of the city of Bonn, is a dominantly Pleistocene group of 240 scoria cones, maars, and small stratovolcanoes covering an area of about 600 km2. The smaller, but better known, East Eifel Volcanic Field is about 40 km NE.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 600 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Chaîne des Puys, prominent in the history of volcanology, form a N-S-trending chain of basaltic and trachytic cinder cones, basaltic maars, and trachytic lava domes in France's Massif Central that has been active into the Holocene.
Type: Lava dome(s); Elevation: 1464 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Olot volcanic field (also known as the Garrotxa volcanic field) occupies the NE corner of Spain south of the Pyrenees Mountains about 90 km NNE of Barcelona. The field consists of a large number of Strombolian pyroclastic cones and associated alkali basaltic lava flows, and is part of the NE Volcanic Province, whic…
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 893 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
The Calatrava volcanic field lies in central Spain near Ciudad Real. The more than 300 basaltic-to-foiditic pyroclastic cones, maars, and lava domes cover an area of more than 5,000 km2.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1117 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Colli Albani (Alban Hills) complex immediately SE of Rome contains a large Pleistocene stratovolcano with a 10 x 12 km caldera formed during an eruptive period with six major explosions that produced at least 280 km3 of ejecta between about 560,000 and 350,000 years ago.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 949 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Campi Flegrei is a 13-km-wide caldera that encompasses part of Naples and extends to the south beneath the Gulf of Pozzuoli. Episodes of significant uplift and subsidence within the dominantly trachytic caldera have occurred since Roman times. The earliest known eruptive products are dated 47,000 years BP.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 458 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

One of the world's most noted volcanoes, Vesuvius (Vesuvio) forms a dramatic backdrop to the Bay of Naples. The active cone was constructed within a large caldera of the older Monte Somma edifice, thought to have formed incrementally beginning about 17,000 years ago.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1281 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Palinuro seamount in the Tyrrhenian Sea north of the Eolian Islands rises nearly 3,000 m to within 70 m of the surface and has an open summit crater. A marine ash layer (PL-1) radiocarbon dated (calibrated) at 9,990 +/- 90 years ago is chemically and stratigraphically similar to two ash layers on land in southern Italy…
Type: Compound; Elevation: -70 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Ischia volcanic complex forms a rectangular, 6 x 9 km island immediately SW of the Campi Flegrei area at the western side of the Bay of Naples. The eruption of the trachytic Green Tuff ignimbrite about 56,000 years ago was followed by caldera formation.
Type: Complex; Elevation: 789 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The mostly submerged Panarea volcanic complex lies about midway between Stromboli and Lipari in the eastern part of the Aeolian Islands. Panarea, the smallest island in the Aeolian Archipelago, lies on the western side of a shallow platform whose shelf margin is at about 130 m depth.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 399 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Lipari, the largest of the Aeolian Islands, is located immediately north of Vulcano Island. The irregular-shaped island contains numerous small stratovolcanoes, craters, and lava domes on a basement of submarine volcanic deposits.
Type: Stratovolcano(es); Elevation: 590 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Spectacular incandescent nighttime explosions at Stromboli have long attracted visitors to the "Lighthouse of the Mediterranean" in the NE Aeolian Islands. This volcano has lent its name to the frequent mild explosive activity that has characterized its eruptions throughout much of historical time.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 924 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The word volcano is derived from Vulcano stratovolcano in Italy's Aeolian Islands. Vulcano was constructed during six stages over the past 136,000 years. Two overlapping calderas, the 2.5-km-wide Caldera del Piano on the SE and the 4-km-wide Caldera della Fossa on the NW, were formed at about 100,000 and 24,000-15,000…
Type: Stratovolcano(es); Elevation: 500 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Mount Etna, on the island of Sicily, has one of the world's longest documented records of volcanism, dating back to 1500 BCE. Basaltic lava flows cover much of the surface of this massive volcano, whose edifice is the highest and most voluminous in Italy.
Type: Stratovolcano(es); Elevation: 3357 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The island of Pantelleria is constructed above a drowned continental rift in the Strait of Sicily and has been the locus of intensive volcano-tectonic activity. Two large Pleistocene calderas dominate the island, which contains numerous post-caldera lava domes and cinder cones and is the type locality for peralkaline r…
Type: Shield; Elevation: 836 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Campi Flegrei del Mar di Sicilia

Campi Flegrei del Mar di Sicilia (Phlegraean Fields of the Sicily Sea) is composed of a group of submarine volcanoes SW of Sicily. The volcanoes were constructed within a submarine depression about 1 km deep in the Strait of Sicily between the SW coast of Sicily and the NE tip of Tunisia, forming submarine banks that a…
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: -8 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Methana volcano consists of a basaltic andesite to rhyodacitic lava dome complex forming the Methana Peninsula in the Sarronian Gulf on the NE side of Peloponnesus. Potassium-Argon ages for the older part of the complex range from 900,000 to 550,000 years, although activity may have begun during the late Pliocene.
Type: Lava dome(s); Elevation: 380 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Mílos and adjacent small islands have grown from submarine and subaerial volcanism that initially was dominantly andesitic and basaltic, but ended with predominately rhyolitic eruptions.
Type: Stratovolcano(es); Elevation: 751 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Santorini (Thera), in the Aegean Sea, has steep-walled caldera rim with villages that overlook an active volcanic island in the center of a caldera bay. The circular island group is composed of overlapping shield volcanoes cut by at least four partially overlapping calderas.
Type: Shield(s); Elevation: 367 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The easternmost volcano of the Aegean arc forms the 9-km-wide island of Nisyros, which is truncated by a 3-4 km wide caldera. The island was constructed during the past 150,000 years, with three cone-building stages including explosive and effusive andesitic eruptions and effusive and extrusive dacitic and rhyolitic ac…
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 698 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
The Kula volcanic field, the westernmost area of young volcanism in Turkey, lies about 450 km WNW of its closest Holocene neighbor in central Turkey, the Karapinar volcanic field.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 750 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Hasandag-Keçiboyduran volcanic complex in Central Anatolia includes the massive double-peaked Hasan Dagi stratovolcano, which has undergone four episodes of caldera collapse, the latest of which formed a 4-5 km wide caldera at the summit.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 3253 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Karaca Dag (also known as Karacalidag) is a broad basaltic shield volcano in SE Turkey about 100 km N of the Syrian border. The volcano lies on the Arabian foreland about 150 km SW of the boundary with the Anatolian Plate and has been active since the Pliocene along a N-S-trending set of fissures and craters associated…
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1957 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Erciyes Volcanic Complex at the northern end of the Sultansazligi Basin in central Anatolia is dominated by the massive eroded Erciyes Dagi stratovolcano at the approximate center of a radial monogenetic volcanic field 32 km in diameter, extending further towards the N. Uslular et al.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 3864 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Nemrut Dagi is the westernmost of a group of volcanoes near Lake Van in eastern Anatolia and the only one that has erupted in historical time. It contains a 9 x 5 km caldera partially filled on its western side by a caldera lake.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2948 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Tendürek Dagi, also known as Tendürük Dagi, is an elongated shield volcano that rises above the Dogubayazit plain, near the Iranian border south of Mount Ararat. An E-W summit ridge, developed north of an arcuate caldera structure exposed only on the southern side, contains two well-developed cones.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 3514 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Mount Ararat, also known as Agri Dagi, is Turkey's highest and largest volume volcano. The overall massif extends ~25 km NW-SE, and 18 km NE-SW, with another large volcano, Kucuk Ararat (or Lesser Ararat), ~11 km SE.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 5165 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Elbrus, the highest peak of the Caucasus Mountains of SW Russia, is a large glaciated stratovolcano. The summit area has two distinct peaks about 1 km apart, with a 250-m-wide crater on the eastern cone, separated by a low saddle from the western peak.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 5642 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
The glacier-covered Kazbek stratovolcano in the Caucasus Mountains of Georgia, just south of the border with Russia, has produced long lava flows down flank valleys.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 5004 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Samsari Volcanic Center consists of more than 20 volcanoes extending about 40 km N-S along the Samsari Ridge, part of the Dzhakheti Highland of southern Georgia, about 90 km WSW of Tbilisi. The most prominent volcanoes are Shavnabada in the north, the Samsari Caldera, and Didi-Abuli in the south.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 3290 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Aragats is a large andesitic-to-dacitic stratovolcano in NW Armenia about 40 km NW of the capital city of Yerevan. The main edifice is dissected by glaciers and is of Pliocene-to-Pleistocene age.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 4095 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Ghegham Volcanic Ridge, located in west-central Armenia between the capital city of Yerevan and Lake Sevan, contains as many as 127 volcanic centers, lava domes and pyroclastic cones, of Pleistocene-to-Holocene age.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 3597 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Vaiyots-Sar pyroclastic cone is located in the southern Armenia province of Vayots Dzor in the western Vardenis Volcanic Highland south of Lake Sevan (Karakhanian et al., 2002); previous names such as Dar-Alages or Daly-Tapa are of Russian origin.
Type: Pyroclastic cone(s); Elevation: 2575 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The mid-Pleistocene Porak volcano lies in the Vardenis volcanic highland about 20 km SE of Lake Sevan. The volcanic field straddles the Armenia/Azerbaijan border, and lava flows extend into both countries. The flanks contain 10 satellitic cones and fissure vents.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 3029 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Tskhouk-Karckar volcano group of cones and lava flows is located in the NW and central part of the Syunik Volcanic Upland along the Armenia/Azerbaijan border about 60 km SE of Lake Sevan. It was constructed within offset segments of the major Pambak-Sevan-Syunik strike-slip fault trending SE from Lake Sevan.
Type: Pyroclastic cone(s); Elevation: 3139 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Red Sea Rift Volcanic Province, Yemen

The basaltic Jebel at Tair volcano rises from 1,200 m depth in the south-central Red Sea, forming an oval-shaped island about 3 km long. It is the northernmost known Holocene volcano in the Red Sea and lies SW of the Farisan Islands.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 244 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Red Sea Rift Volcanic Province, Yemen

Zukur (Zugar), the northernmost large island of the Zukur-Hanish island group in the southern Red Sea, is formed of Holocene basaltic pyroclastic cones and spatter cones that issued youthful-looking pahoehoe lava flows. This island group lies in shallow waters S of the Red Sea median trough.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 624 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Red Sea Rift Volcanic Province, Yemen

The Hanish Islands are formed from a series of volcanic vents along a NE-SW trend, and include the Holocene Great Hanish, Little Hanish, and many other small islands and submarine shoals. The Zukur-Hanish island group lies in shallow waters S of the Red Sea median trough.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 422 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Red Sea Rift Volcanic Province, Yemen

The 5-km-long Jebel Zubair Island is the largest of a group of small islands and submerged shoals that rise from a shallow platform in the Red Sea rift. The platform and eruptive vents forming the islands and shoals are oriented NNW-SSE, parallel to the rift.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 191 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

Numerous phreatic explosion craters are present across the Salt Plain NNE of the Erta Ale Range in one of the lowest areas of the desolate Danakil depression. The most recent of these craters, Dallol, lies 48 m below sea level and was formed during an eruption in 1926.
Type: Explosion crater(s); Elevation: -48 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Alid is an isolated, dissected volcano in the central Danakil depression. Elongated in an E-W direction perpendicular to the orientation of the Alid graben, it consists of a structural dome of uplifted sedimentary rocks rising 700 m above the graben floor, which was produced by intrusion of a silicic magma body.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 904 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Gada Ale (also known as Kebrit Ale), the most prominent volcano at the northern end of the Erta Ale Range, is formed of interstratified lava flows and hyaloclastites. Fumarolic activity is continuing, and the summit crater contains a small lake with hot mud.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 287 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The summit region of Alu, ~5 km NW of the Dalafilla stratovolcano, is an ellipsoidal volcanic horst, elongated NNW-SSE, and formed primarily of older basaltic lava flows. Recent fractures along the axis of the Erta Ale range cut the main horst of Alu and areas to the SSE.
Type: Fissure vent(s); Elevation: 578 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
Bora Ale is a complex volcano located near the center of the Erta Ale Range. The earliest activity formed submarine lava flows partially covered by Quaternary reef deposits.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 668 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The Erta Ale basaltic shield volcano in Ethiopia has a 50-km-wide edifice that rises more than 600 m from below sea level in the Danakil depression. The volcano includes a 0.7 x 1.6 km summit crater hosting steep-sided pit craters.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 585 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Hayli Gubbi is the southernmost volcano of the Erta Ale Range. Recent tectonism has created a NW-SE graben across the summit, with a 380-m-diameter scoria cone at the summit and a 260-m-diameter crater displaying fumarolic activity.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 493 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Ale Bagu, also known as Ummuna, is an elongated stratovolcano located SW of Erta Ale volcano. In contrast to other volcanoes of the Erta Ale Range, it is located SW of the axis of the range, and is mantled by basaltic pyroclastic rocks. Summit craters are elongated along a NNW-SSE trend.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 988 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The Nabro stratovolcano is the highest volcano in the Danakil depression of northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, at the SE end of the Danakil Alps. Nabro, along with Mallahle, Asavyo, and Sork Ale volcanoes, collectively comprise the Bidu volcanic complex SW of Dubbi volcano.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2218 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Mallahle is the central of three NE-SW-trending stratovolcanoes (along with Asavyo and Nabro) in the Danakil horst SW of Dubbi volcano. These volcanoes, plus Sork'Ale, form the Bidu Volcanic Complex. The volcano is truncated by a steep-walled 6-km-wide caldera, and is formed of rhyolitic lava flows and pyroclastics.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1875 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Sork Ale is a silicic stratovolcano located in the Danakil horst SW of Dubbi volcano. Also known as Asdaga, it was constructed perpendicular to the NE-SW orientation of three larger stratovolcanoes (Nabro, Mallahle, and Asavyo) with which it forms the Bidu Volcanic Complex at the southern end of the Danakil Alps.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1611 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Asavyo, also known as Bara’Ale, is the SW-most of three large silicic stratovolcanoes (along with Mallahle and Nabro) constructed along a NE-SW-trending line in the Danakil horst. A large 12-km-wide caldera truncates the summit. Basaltic lava flows cover the flanks, which merge into the Mogorros plains to the south.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1338 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Mat Ala is a low shield volcano in the southern Tat Ali Range, east of Afderà volcano. A 300-m-deep, 2.5 x 3.5 km wide caldera is found at the summit of the volcano, whose flanks are cut by numerous N-S-trending faults.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 493 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Tat Ali volcano is the dominant feature of the Tat Ali Range, east of Lake Afrera. The low Holocene shield volcano has an elongated summit depression and has produced a variety of rock types, ranging from basalts to pantellerites.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 655 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Borawli stratovolcano rises above the eastern shore of Lake Afrera, also known as Lake Giulietti. The upper part of the conical edifice consists of trachytic lava flows overlying older basaltic flows.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 784 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
Dubbi, located east of the Erta Ale Range and south of the crystalline basement rocks of the Danakil Alps, is a large volcanic massif that rises above the western shore of the Red Sea.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1625 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The Ma Alalta stratovolcano, also known as Pierre Pruvost, is located well to the west of the Danakil depression at the foot of the regional Ethiopian scarp, between two large horsts of uplifted basement blocks.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1745 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The massive Alayta shield volcano covers an area of 2700 km2 in the western Danakil depression SW of Lake Afrera. A series of very recent craters is aligned along the NNW-trending axis of the basaltic-to-trachytic shield.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1496 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Dabbahu (also known as Boina, Boyna, or Moina) is a Pleistocene-to-Holocene volcanic massif forming an axial range of the Afar depression SSW of the Alayta massif. Late-stage pantelleritic obsidian flows, lava domes, and pumice cones form the summit and upper flanks.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1401 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Dabbayra, the westernmost volcano of the Afar depression, was constructed along an offshoot of the Ethiopian escarpment, SW of the Teru plain. In contrast to structural trends in other parts of Afar, Dabbayra (also known as Bar-Ali) consists of a basaltic shield volcano elongated ENE-WSW.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1302 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

As the southernmost axial range of western Afar, the Manda Hararo complex is located in the Kalo plain, SSE of Dabbahu volcano. The massive 105-km-long and 20-30 km wide complex represents an uplifted segment of a mid-ocean ridge spreading center.
Type: Shield(s); Elevation: 600 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Groppo was identified by IAVCEI (1973) as a small alkali rhyolitic stratovolcano located in the western Afar near the Ethiopian escarpment, NE of Dessye. However, the nearest volcanic feature, identified in satellite imagery about 15 km NW from the given location, is a dark lava-flow field about 2.5 x 4.5 km in size, s…
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 852 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Afderà is an isolated rhyolitic stratovolcano located between the Erta Ale, Tat Ali, and Alayta ranges. It lies at the intersection of three fault systems. Young rhyolitic lava domes are aligned N-S at its southern foot. Only a few late-stage satellitic cones are of basaltic composition.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1250 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The Manda Gargori rift, located north of the town of Aisa Aita NE of Borawli volcano and SE of Kurub volcano, is the youngest rift segment in the Afar depression and is only one third the width of the adjacent Manda Hararo-Goba'ad rift system to the west.
Type: Fissure vent(s); Elevation: 700 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

Manda-Inakir consists of a series of NW-trending fissure vents and pyroclastic cones along the Ethiopia-Djibouti border. The elongated complex represents an uplifted mid-ocean ridge spreading center now exposed above sea level.
Type: Fissure vent(s); Elevation: 600 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The Mousa Alli volcanic complex is a large Holocene stratovolcano constructed along the border between Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Djibouti. The trachytic-to-rhyolitic volcano is the most prominent topographic feature in this area.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1993 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
The Gufa volcanic field, located along the Eritrea-Djibouti border, consists of a group of basaltic scoria cones and lava flows, aligned E-W, NE of the large Mousa Alli stratovolcano.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 600 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The Assab volcanic field near the Red Sea coast in southern Eritrea forms a spectacular range of basaltic cinder cones and associated lava flows. The massive lava field covers a 55 x 90 km area, and flows reached the Red Sea along a broad front.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 987 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The Ardoukôba (Asal) Rift in Djibouti, trending NW from the Red Sea, contains a broad area of youthful fissure vents between Lake Asal and the Ghoubbat al Kharab gulf. It is subaerially exposed over 12 km between these two bodies of water and contains numerous basaltic cinder and spatter cones.
Type: Fissure vent(s); Elevation: 298 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The small Holocene shield volcano, also known as Kurub Koma, Kurub Koba, or Curub, lies in the Saha Plain, SE of the Manda Hararo complex in the South Danakil region. The easternmost lava flow was potassium-argon dated at about 0.3 million years.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 625 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

Dama Ali is a broad 25-km-wide shield volcano that rises above the NW shore of Lake Abbe in eastern Ethiopia. Nested circular craters are located at the summit of the dominantly basaltic volcano, which also displays an older caldera rim.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1068 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

Yangudi volcano, lying in the Addado graben of the northern Main Ethiopian Rift, is a complex rhyolitic stratovolcano with an elliptical summit caldera. A trachytic lava flow originating in the caldera covers part of the southern flank of Yangudi, also known as Angudi, Jangudi, or Langudi.
Type: Complex; Elevation: 1383 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

Gabillema is a rhyolitic stratovolcano along the axis of the Addado graben. The volcano was constructed at the intersection of the central Afar rift zone with the northern end of the Main Ethiopian Rift.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1459 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

Ayelu is a vegetated rhyolitic stratovolcano, located south of the Asbahri plain in the southern Afar region. On its eastern side, 2145-m-high Ayelu is cut by regional faults and is overlain by ignimbrites erupted from Adwa volcano immediately to the east.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2145 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

Hertali is a basaltic fissure vent that fed lava flows at the S end of the Awash plain, about 50 km NNE of Dofen volcano. It was considered by Mohr and Wood (1976) to have been active during the late Pleistocene to Holocene on the basis of its youthful-looking morphology.
Type: Fissure vent; Elevation: 900 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Liado Hayk (Liado Lake) volcanic field consists of a dozen closely spaced maars and cinder cones with associated lava fields in the Awash plain NE of Dofen volcano. The morphology of the cones and maars suggested a late Pleistocene or Holocene age (Wood, 1979 p.c.).
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 878 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

Adwa (also known as Aabida, Amoissa, or Dabita), is a broad stratovolcano in the southern Afar area immediately east of the younger vegetated Ayelu volcano. It has a roughly 3 x 4 km caldera that originated following eruption of voluminous ignimbrites, with a trachytic dome extruded in the eastern part of the caldera.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1670 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Dofen shield volcano rises 450 m above the Awash plain in the northern Main Ethiopian Rift. Numerous cinder cones, constructed along a 10-km-long, N-S-trending line, occur on the flanks of the dominantly rhyolitic volcano.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1151 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia
An area of Holocene basaltic lava flows is located along the Main Ethiopian Rift at Beru, between Fentale and Kone (Gariboldi) volcanoes.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1100 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

Fentale is a volcanic complex at the N end of the Main Ethiopian Rift that includes a main stratovolcano and caldera with various subsidiary features. Products are primarily rhyolitic obsidian lava flows with minor tuffs.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2007 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Kone volcanic complex (also known as Gariboldi) is composed of a series of silicic calderas and young basaltic cinder cones and lava flows about 30 km SW of Fentale volcano in the Main Ethiopian Rift. As many as eight silicic calderas are accompanied by ignimbrite outflow sheets.
Type: Caldera(s); Elevation: 1380 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia
The Boset volcanic complex includes the Boset-Gudda (Great Boset) and Boset-Bericha (Little Boset) composite volcanoes rising above the floor of the Ethiopian Rift valley.
Type: Stratovolcano(es); Elevation: 2447 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Bishoftu volcanic field, also known as Debre Zeit, consists of an area of fissure-fed Holocene lava flows, cinder cones, tuff rings, and maars. Several of the maars are filled by lakes, which are popular recreational destinations from the nearby capital city of Addis Ababa.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1850 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Melkassa (or Sodore) volcanic field is an extensive 15 x 25 km group of about 30 Pleistocene and Holocene pyroclastic cones and lava flows that covers the floor of the E side of the Ethiopian Rift Valley, around the town of Melkassa, between the Boset volcanic complex and Gedamsa caldera.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1765 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Gedemsa caldera covers 7 x 9 km along the Main Ethiopian Rift E of Lake Koka and SW of Wonji Sugar Estate Farm. The steep-sided edifice has walls 100-200 m high whose upper part consists primarily of rhyolitic lava flows, formed by the eruption of a series of trachytic ignimbrites, It is also cut by many NNE-SSW-tr…
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 1909 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Bora-Bericha-Tullu Moye (BBTM) volcanic complex includes three main silicic edifices and at least 11 smaller cones within the Main Ethiopian Rift. Tullu Moye is a youthful trachytic-to-rhyolitic pumice cone with a 700-m-wide summit crater.
Type: Pyroclastic cone; Elevation: 2345 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

A large area of basaltic cinder cones and lava flows lies within about 5 km of the SE shore of Lake Ziway, and also forms islands along its E shore. About 80 vents were formed along the East Ziway segment of the Wonji Fault Belt.
Type: Fissure vent(s); Elevation: 1889 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Butajiri-Silti volcanic field consists of a large group of basaltic cinder cones, maars, and lava flows in an 80-km-long, NE-SW-trending area near the western margin of the Ethiopian Rift. At least 13 maars, many filled by lakes, are located near the town of Debre Zeit, SE of the capital city of Addis Ababa.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 2281 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia
Aluto, between lakes Zway and Langano (Mirrga), is a stratovolcano with multiple vents aligned along NNE-SSW and E-W fissures along a narrow graben between the two lakes.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2335 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Shala (also known as O'a) caldera along the central Main Ethiopian Rift forms the eastern portion of the 15 x 25 km Lake Shala. Formation of the caldera about 240,000 years ago was accompanied by the eruption of two ignimbrite deposits, the first of which was strongly welded.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 2075 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

Corbetti is one of the largest calderas (15.6 x 10.9 km) within the Main Ethiopian Rift (MER). As summarized by Colby et al. (2022), it has followed an evolutionary pattern similar to other caldera volcanoes within the MER, beginning with a shield-building phase of peralkaline rhyolite lava flows, followed by at least…
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 2289 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Main Ethiopian Rift Volcanic Province, Ethiopia

The Bilate River basin west of Lake Awasa contains a group of lake-filled maars and tuff rings of Pleistocene and probable Holocene age (WoldeGabriel 1987, pers. comm.). Active hot springs and fumaroles are located in this area.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1700 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Korath Range is an isolated group of about 20 tuff cones and lava flows in southern Ethiopia that were erupted along the Turkana Rift, which extends north from Kenya. Many of the cones issued lava flows from their flanks that traveled up to about 5 km.
Type: Tuff cone(s); Elevation: 912 m; Setting: Rift zone / Intermediate crust (15-25 km)

The 2-km-wide North Island in Lake Turkana is the northernmost and smallest of three volcanic islands in the lake. It is primarily composed of trachyandesitic-to-trachytic phreatomagmatic deposits from overlapping eroded tuff cones or tuff rings.
Type: Tuff cone(s); Elevation: 490 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Central Island in the middle of Lake Turkana, also known as Crocodile Island, is composed of more than a dozen craters and cones, three of which are filled by small lakes. The two largest lakes partially fill craters up to 1 km wide and about 80 m deep.
Type: Tuff cone(s); Elevation: 518 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Marsabit is a massive basaltic shield volcano located 170 km E off the center of the East African Rift. There are 22 maars and 180 cinder cones on its slopes, most of which are concentrated along NW- and NE-trending belts that cut across the thickly vegetated summit region.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1707 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The southernmost and largest of the three volcanic islands in Lake Turkana, South Island (sometimes referred to as Hohnel Island), contains numerous tuff cones. Early stage cone formation may have been associated with a high stand of Lake Turkana dated at about 10,000 years ago, and later subaerial activity postdates t…
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 800 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Barrier volcanic complex separates Lake Turkana from the broad Suguta Trough to the S, the site of a former lake. The volcano is comprised of four overlapping shield volcanoes, with the youngest, Kakorinya, located over the axis of the East African Rift.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1032 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Namarunu trachytic shield volcano along the axis of the East African Rift is topped by late Pleistocene and Holocene cones and lava flows. Though largely Pliocene, voluminous basaltic effusive and explosive activity took place during the early Holocene on the lower N, E, and S flanks.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 817 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

A large number of late-Pleistocene to Holocene basaltic cones, lava flows, and maars occur along a roughly 50-km-long NE-SW trend on the Segererua and Rusarus Plateaus and areas to the SW. This volcanic region is located well E of the East African Rift, S of the massive Marsabit shield volcano.
Type: Pyroclastic cone(s); Elevation: 699 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The broad Emuruangogolak shield volcano is situated at a narrow constriction in the Gregory Rift and almost completely straddles it. A 5 x 3.5 km summit caldera formed about 38,000 years ago. Since then trachytic and basaltic lava flows were erupted on the northern and southern flanks and within the caldera.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1285 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The 30-km-wide Silali trachytic shield volcano, the largest Quaternary volcano in the northern Gregory Rift, completely straddles the East African Rift. The 5 x 8 km summit caldera with 300 m deep walls is thought to have formed incrementally about 63,000 years ago, related to eruption of the Kantenmening basaltic and…
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1528 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The dominantly Pleistocene Paka shield volcano in the Gregory Rift contains a small 1.5-km-wide summit caldera. Eruption of large volumes of trachytic pyroclastic rocks around the end of the Pleistocene and the beginning of the Holocene formed a NW-trending ridge of pyroclastic cones across the summit region; collapse…
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1697 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The trachytic Korosi shield volcano lies at the N end of Lake Baringo. Unlike other rift valley volcanoes, it does not contain a summit caldera. Lava domes on the N flanks have fed trachytic lava flows.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1446 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The elongated Ol Kokwe Island in the center of Lake Baringo SW of Korosi volcano consists of young basaltic scoria cones that cap a trachytic shield volcano. N-S-trending faults cut the complex, producing W-facing scarps.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1130 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The broad NE-SW-trending Nyambeni shield volcano is capped by numerous phonolitic lava domes, basaltic cones, and lava flows of late-Pleistocene to Holocene age (Hackman et al., 1989). The basaltic cinder cones are the youngest features.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 750 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The massive Menengai shield volcano occupies the floor of the East African Rift. Construction of a 30 km3 shield volcano beginning about 200,000 years ago was followed by the eruption of two voluminous ash-flow tuffs, each preceded by major pumice falls.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 2278 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Elmenteita Badlands, located between Lake Elmenteita (N) and Eburru volcano (S), is an area of pyroclastic cones and lava flows of varying ages. Large basaltic lava flows and ash cones post-date the 10,000-year-old high-stand of Lake Elmenteita (Thomson and Dodson, 1963).
Type: Pyroclastic cone(s); Elevation: 2126 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Homa Mountain is a large carbonatitic complex with a flat-topped summit that forms a broad peninsula on the E shore of Lake Victoria. This dominantly Miocene-to-Pleistocene complex contains numerous flank vents, including the carbonatitic and ultramafic Lake Simbi maar on the lower E flank.
Type: Complex; Elevation: 1751 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Eburru volcano is elongated E-W perpendicular to the Gregory Rift NW of Lake Naivasha. The main edifice is eroded, but young partly vegetated rhyolitic domes occur on the E flank and are probably of Holocene age (Thompson and Dodson, 1963).
Type: Complex; Elevation: 2856 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Olkaria volcanic complex, located immediately S of Lake Naivasha and W of Longonot volcano, comprises up to 80 individual alkali rhyolite centers. A thick, geochemically diverse basal complex is overlain by a dominantly silicic lava-dome and lava-flow complex constructed within a largely obscured 11 x 7.5-km-wide c…
Type: Pyroclastic cone(s); Elevation: 2434 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The trachytic Longonot stratovolcano SE of Lake Naivasha in the Gregory Rift valley contains a 8 x 12 km caldera. Formation of the caldera accompanied large explosive eruptions about 21,000 years ago.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2776 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The phonolitic-to-trachytic Suswa volcano in the Kenyan Rift, ~50 km WNW of Nairobi, is notable for its 8 x 12 km caldera. Construction of an early shield volcano was followed by eruption of voluminous Pleistocene pumice and lava flows that accompanied incremental formation of the caldera.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 2356 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The symmetrical Ol Doinyo Lengai is the only volcano where the eruption of carbonatite tephras and lavas has been observed. The prominent stratovolcano, known to the Maasai as "The Mountain of God," rises above the broad plain south of Lake Natron in the Gregory Rift Valley.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2962 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The 100-km-long NW-SE-trending Chyulu Hills volcanic field is located 150 km E of the Kenya Rift. It contains several hundred small cones and flows, including numerous recent cinder cones. Two of these, Shaitani and Chainu, erupted during the mid-19th century.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 2188 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Ngozi caldera is the most prominent volcanic feature of the Poroto Ridge, a transverse structure at the northern end of the Karonga basin. The trachytic-to-phonolitic volcano contains a 3-km-wide caldera with a 1.5 x 2.5 km lake in the southern part of the caldera that is bounded by steep-walled cliffs 150-300 m high.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 2614 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Rungwe volcano, the largest in the Karonga basin NW of Lake Malawi (Lake Nyasa), is cut by a 4-km-wide caldera that is breached to the WSW. Hummocky terrain from a debris-avalanche deposit produced by collapse of the summit and western flank extends at least 20 km SW of the volcano.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2953 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Meru has a conical profile when viewed from the west, but there is a 4-km-wide collapse crater to the E. The summit collapse is associated with the early Holocene Momella event that resulted in debris avalanche and lahar deposits as far as the W flank of Kilimanjaro.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 4550 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Late-stage activity of the Kyejo (Kieyo) trachytic stratovolcano, NW of Lake Malawi (Lake Nyassa), consisted of the formation of numerous maars and cinder cones. This stratovolcano is elongated in a NW-SE direction and has been active since the mid-Pleistocene.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2176 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The carbonatite lavas and tuffs of the Fort Portal Volcanic Field in Uganda, NE of Mount Ruwenzori between Lake Albert and Lake Edward, consists of a group of tuff cones and maars covering an area of about 145 km2.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1615 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Ndali-Kasenda Volcanic Field (also known as Kwatya) is located in the Western Rift Valley, N of the equator and E of the Ruwenzori Mountains about halfway between Lake Edward and Lake Albert. The numerous tuff cones and lake-filled maars are part of a group of Quaternary volcanic fields in western Uganda.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1300 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Albertine Rift Volcanic Province, DR Congo

Africa's most active volcano, Nyamulagira (also known as Nyamuragira), is a massive high-potassium basaltic shield about 25 km N of Lake Kivu and 13 km NNW of the steep-sided Nyiragongo volcano. The summit is truncated by a small 2 x 2.3 km caldera that has walls up to about 100 m high.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 3058 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Albertine Rift Volcanic Province, DR Congo

The Nyiragongo stratovolcano contained a lava lake in its deep summit crater that was active for half a century before draining catastrophically through its outer flanks in 1977. The steep slopes contrast to the low profile of its neighboring shield volcano, Nyamuragira.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 3470 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Albertine Rift Volcanic Province, DR Congo-Rwanda

Karisimbi is a complex basanitic-to-trachytic volcano with a symmetrical sharp-peaked summit. The 2-km-wide Branca caldera, located SE of the summit, is filled by viscous lava flows and two explosion craters. The large 1.2-km-wide Muntango pit crater is located south of the summit.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 4490 m; Setting: Rift zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Western Africa Volcanic Province, Equatorial Guinea

Pico Basilé is the largest and highest of three basaltic shield volcanoes forming Bioko Island. Lying on the continental shelf along the Cameroon Line, this volcano is modified by the same NNE faults as Mt. Cameroon across the Gulf of Guinea on the mainland.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 2999 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Young cinder cones and maars are abundant in the low-lying Tombel Graben (also referred to as the Tombel Plain) between Mount Cameroon and Mount Manengouba (within 4°58'N, 9°51'E and 4°33'N, 9°35'E). Mount Koupe, composed of Tertiary syenite, dominates the area.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 500 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The massive steep-sided Mount Cameroon rises above the coast of west Cameroon, overlooking the Bight of Biafra, part of the Gulf of Guinea. The dominantly basaltic-to-trachybasaltic edifice forms a volcanic horst constructed above a basement of Precambrian metamorphic rocks covered with Cretaceous to Quaternary sedimen…
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 4095 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Numerous maars and basaltic cinder cones lie on or near the deeply dissected rhyolitic and trachytic Mount Oku massif along the Cameroon volcanic line. The Mount Oku stratovolcano is cut by a large caldera.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 3011 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
West Central Sahara Volcanic Province, Niger

The Todra Volcanic Field covers about 1,000 km2 in the Tuareg shield in the southern Aïr region of Niger. Activity began with the eruption of about 30 trachytic and phonolitic volcanoes through Precambrian basement rocks.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1780 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
West Central Sahara Volcanic Province, Algeria

The large E-W elongated Tahalra volcanic field covers an area of about 1,800 km2 in the Hoggar Province of southern Algeria. It lies WSW of the town of Tamanrasset and was active from the Miocene to the Holocene, producing alkaline Strombolian cones and lava flows.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1467 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
West Central Sahara Volcanic Province, Algeria

The massive Atakor volcanic field is the largest in the Hoggar (or Ahaggar) volcanic province of southern Algeria and covers an area of 2,150 km2. Quaternary basaltic (mostly basanitic) scoria cones and lava flows lie near older trachytic and phonolitic lava domes and volcanic necks that form some of the most dramatic…
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 2918 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
West Central Sahara Volcanic Province, Algeria

The Manzaz volcanic field, north of the Atakor volcanic field in the Hoggar (Ahaggar) volcanic province of Algeria, consists of a large number of scoria cones and associated lava flows. The field covers an area of 1,500 km2, overlying Precambrian metamorphic and plutonic rocks of the Tuareg shield.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1672 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
East Central Sahara Volcanic Province, Chad

The Tarso Tôh Pleistocene-to-Holocene volcanic field in the NW part of the arid Tibesti Range of Chad contains 150 scoria cones and two maars. Basaltic lava flows fill valleys and plains over an area of 80 km in an E-W direction and 20-30 km in a N-S direction in the area north of the more well-known Tarso Toussidé Vol…
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 2000 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
East Central Sahara Volcanic Province, Chad

Tarso Toussidé, a broad volcanic massif at the western end of the Tibesti Range, is capped by the Toussidé stratovolcano, constructed at the western end of the 14-km-wide ignimbritic Pleistocene Yirrigue caldera.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 3299 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
East Central Sahara Volcanic Province, Chad
The large Emi Koussi volcano at the SE end of the Tibesti Range, a 60 x 80 km massif constructed over a basement of Cretaceous and Paleozoic sandstones, forms the highest summit of the Sahara.
Type: Shield(pyroclastic); Elevation: 3415 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
East Central Sahara Volcanic Province, Chad

The broad summit of Tarso Voon volcano, located in the west-central part of the Tibesti Range, is truncated by a shallow 14 x 18 km wide caldera. Ignimbrite deposits surround the caldera to distances of 15-35 km. It was constructed over a basement of Precambrian schists.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 3100 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The most prominent feature of the vast Jebel Marra volcanic field, located in the Darfur province of western Sudan, is the youthful Deriba caldera. The 5-km-wide, steep-walled caldera, located at the southern end of the field, was formed about 3,500 years ago at the time of the eruption of voluminous airfall pumice and…
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 3042 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The basaltic Kutum volcanic field, in the northern Darfur area of western Sudan, is located SW of the larger Meidob volcanic field. As with other Saharan volcanic fields, Kutum (also known as the Tagabo Hills or Berti Hills) contains very well-preserved cones, lava flows, and explosion craters.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1779 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The alkaline Meidob volcanic field in western Sudan, at the NE end of the Darfur volcanic province, covers an area of 5,000 km2 with nearly 700 Pliocene-to-Holocene vents. The field was constructed over an uplifted Precambrian igneous and metamorphic basement and is elongated in an E-W direction.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 2000 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Bayuda volcanic field is located in the Bayuda Desert of NE Sudan, south of the major Abu Hamed bend of the Nile River about 300 km N of Khartoum. More than 90 eruptive centers along a WNW-ESE line were constructed over Precambrian and Paleozoic granitic rocks near the center of the Bayuda Desert.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 670 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Northern Arabia Volcanic Province, Syria-Jordan-Saudi Arabia

The massive Harrat Ash Shaam volcanic province, which extends from Syria through Jordan and into northern Saudi Arabia, contains many smaller volcanic fields. Activity began during the Miocene; a younger eruptive stage, at the SE end of the field, occurred during the late Pleistocene and Holocene (Brown et al., 1984).
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1100 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Western Arabia Volcanic Province, Saudi Arabia

Harrat Lunayyir is a basaltic volcanic field in NW Saudi Arabia, east of the Red Sea port of Umm Lajj. It contains about 50 volcanic cones that were constructed over Precambrian crystalline rocks along a N-S axis.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1370 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Western Arabia Volcanic Province, Saudi Arabia

The 4000 km2 Harrat Ithnayn volcanic field contains scattered shield volcanoes and scoria cones. It merges with the much larger Harrat Khaybar volcanic field to the south. The field overlies Cambrian sandstones and Precambrian basement rocks.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1625 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Western Arabia Volcanic Province, Saudi Arabia

Harrat Khaybar, one of Saudi Arabia's largest volcanic fields, covers an area of more than 14,000 km2 N of Madinah (Medina). A 100-km-long N-S linear vent system contains felsic lava domes, tuff rings, the Jabal Qidr stratovolcano, and numerous small basaltic cones.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 2093 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Western Arabia Volcanic Province, Saudi Arabia

The 5,900 km3 Harrat Kishb volcanic field, located E of a N-S-trending line of volcanic fields in central Saudi Arabia, is comprised of basaltic scoria cones, tuff rings and maars, and phonolitic lava domes and flows.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1475 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Southwest Arabia Volcanic Province, Saudi Arabia

The Harrat al Birk volcanic field, also known as Harrat Hayil or Hubhub al Sheikh, is the only Saudi Arabian volcanic field that lies directly along the Red Sea coast. It covers an 1800 km2 area west of the town of Abha and separates the Tihamat ash Sham and Tihamat 'Asir coastal plains.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 587 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Western Arabia Volcanic Province, Saudi Arabia

Harrat Rahat, Saudi Arabia's largest lava field, covers 20,000 km2 and extends for 300 km S of Madinah (Medina). Four coalescing lava fields erupted from offset NNW-trending vent systems comprise the field, which has an average width of 60 km. Lava flows extend as far as 100 km W of the axis of the field.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1744 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Southwest Arabia Volcanic Province, Saudi Arabia

Jabal Yar, the southernmost young volcanic field in Saudi Arabia, is a small olivine basaltic field along the Red Sea coast at the SW tip of Saudi Arabia. It contains three groups of volcanoes, Qummatain, Djar'atain-Harra, and 'Ukwatain. Hot springs occur south of Djar'atain and between it and 'Ukwatain.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 305 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Quaternary Harra of Arhab in Yemen, north of the capital city of Sana'a, consists of a 1,500 km2 basaltic plateau capped by a few small stratovolcanoes and about 60 scoria cones, two of which have erupted in historical time.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 3100 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Jabal Haylan area contains a 75-km-long chain of tuff cones and associated olivine basaltic lava flows in eastern Yemen. The chain crosses a NW-SE-trending fault extending between the highlands and desert lowlands to the east.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1550 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The lava fields surrounding the town of Dhamar are part of a volcanic field extending 80 km E that includes several stratovolcanoes and many youthful volcanic cones. Basaltic lava flows overlie older rhyolitic flows.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 3500 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Harra es-Sawâd (or Shuqra) volcanic field in southern Yemen extends for nearly 100 km along the Gulf of Aden, east of the city of Shuqra (Shaqra). The field is oriented WSW-ENE and contains about a hundred cones that have sent lava flows across a 40 x 95 km area of faulted basement limestones.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 1737 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Balhaf-Bir Ali Volcanic Field along the Gulf of Aden in southern Yemen contains cinder cones associated with vesicular lava flows and scoria cones. The 500 km2 field lies along the Gulf of Aden about 120 km SW of the city of Al Mukalla. Lava flows covered much of the area and created an irregular shoreline.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 604 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Near the villages of Hleime and Al Ghayl, along the Wadi Hadhramout valley about 45 km from the coast of Yemen, is what appears to be a pyroclastic volcanic cone and extensive dark lava flows.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 464 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The Damavand stratovolcano is located 70 km NE of Iran's capital city of Tehran and 70 km S of the Caspian Sea. A younger cone has been constructed during the past 600,000 years over an older edifice, remnants of which were previously interpreted as a caldera wall.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 5670 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Madagascar-Comoros Volcanic Province, Union of the Comoros

La Grille is a basaltic shield volcano at the N end of Grand Comore Island (Ngazidja). Unlike the larger Karthala volcano to the S, it lacks a summit caldera but has an abundance of pyroclastic cones.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1064 m; Setting: Intraplate / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

Mayotte, located in the Mozambique Channel between the northern tip of Madagascar and the eastern coast of Africa, consists two main volcanic islands, Grande Terre and Petite Terre, and roughly twenty islets within a barrier-reef lagoon complex (Zinke et al., 2005; Pelleter et al., 2014).
Type: Shield; Elevation: 660 m; Setting: Intraplate / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Madagascar-Comoros Volcanic Province, Union of the Comoros

The southernmost and largest of the two shield volcanoes forming Grand Comore Island (also known as Ngazidja Island), Karthala has two overlapping 3-4 km summit calderas generated by repeated collapse.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 2350 m; Setting: Intraplate / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

Piton de la Fournaise is a massive basaltic shield volcano on the French island of Réunion in the western Indian Ocean. Much of its more than 530,000-year history overlapped with eruptions of the deeply dissected Piton des Neiges shield volcano to the NW.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 2632 m; Setting: Intraplate / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Amsterdam-St. Paul Hotspot Volcano Group, France

Boomerang Seamount, an active submarine volcano 18 km NE of Amsterdam Island, was first discovered during a bathymetric survey in 1996. It rises to within 650 m of the ocean surface and has a 2-km-wide summit caldera that is 200 m deep. Rift zones that extend to the SE and N give it an arcuate shape.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: -650 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Amsterdam-St. Paul Hotspot Volcano Group, France

The elliptical 7 x 10 km Amsterdam Island is the northernmost subaerial volcano on the Antarctic Plate. The basaltic volcano is located near the axis of the East Indian Ocean Ridge adjacent to the Indian Plate.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 881 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Amsterdam-St. Paul Hotspot Volcano Group, France

The uninhabited triangular island of St. Paul is located near the axis of the East Indian Ocean Ridge, 80 km S of Amsterdam Island. It is composed of an older tuff cone surmounted by a basaltic stratovolcano with a 1.8-km-wide caldera.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 268 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The McDonald Islands are located on the Kerguelen Plateau about 75 km W of Heard Island. The largest island, McDonald, is composed of a layered phonolitic tuff plateau cut by phonolitic dikes and lava domes.
Type: Complex; Elevation: 263 m; Setting: Intraplate / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

Heard Island on the Kerguelen Plateau in the southern Indian Ocean consists primarily of the emergent portion of two volcanic structures. The large glacier-covered composite basaltic-to-trachytic cone of Big Ben comprises most of the island, and the smaller Mt.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2745 m; Setting: Intraplate / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The Kerguelen Islands are composed primarily of Tertiary flood basalts and a complex of plutonic rocks. The trachybasaltic-to-trachytic Mount Ross stratovolcano at the S end was active during the late Pleistocene.
Type: Stratovolcano(es); Elevation: 1840 m; Setting: Intraplate / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

Ile de l'Est, the easternmost island in the Crozet archipelago, is a glacially eroded basaltic stratovolcano. A metamorphosed gabbroic complex is cut by a dense network of dikes and cone sheets that fed younger volcanic rocks.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1090 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

Île de la Possession, located immediately W of Ile de l'Est in the Crozet archipelago, consists of a stratovolcano intruded by ring and cone dikes and modified by block faulting, marine erosion, and uplift.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 934 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The 8 x 10 km Ile aux Cochons, at the W end of the Crozet Islands, is a single stratovolcano with a small summit caldera and more than 60 scoria cones. The production of phreatomagmatic breccias interbedded with thin lava flows was followed by block faulting and the eruption of scoria cones and lava flows along four ra…
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 775 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Marion Hotspot Volcano Group, South Africa

Uninhabited 5 x 10-km-wide Prince Edward Island lies opposite Marion Island at the N end of a submarine plateau on the Antarctic Plate immediately S of the SW Indian Ocean Ridge. It is a low-angle remnant of a large shield volcano formerly centered off the current NW shore of the island.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 672 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Marion Hotspot Volcano Group, South Africa

Marion Island lies at the SW end of a submarine plateau immediately south of the SW Indian Ocean Ridge, opposite Prince Edward Island. The low profile of the 24-km-wide dominantly basaltic and trachybasaltic volcano is formed by two young shields that rise above a flat-topped submarine platform.
Type: Shield(s); Elevation: 1230 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The 4-km-wide Tuhua/Mayor Island, offshore of North Island in the Bay of Plenty, is the emergent portion of a 15-km-wide peralkaline shield volcano constructed between about 120,000 and 35,000 years ago.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 355 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Western North Island Volcanic Province, New Zealand

The 600 km2 Auckland Volcanic Field, at the south end of the Northland Peninsula, is overlain by New Zealand's largest city, Auckland / Tamaki Makaurau. This northernmost Quaternary volcanic field of the Auckland Intraplate Province is dominated by intraplate alkali basaltic to basanitic rocks.
Type: Volcanic field; Elevation: 260 m; Setting: Intraplate / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Western North Island Volcanic Province, New Zealand

The nearly symmetrical, steep-sided cone of Taranaki (previously known as Egmont), is a large andesitic stratovolcano on the west coast of central North Island. It is surrounded by a ring plain of debris-avalanche and lahar deposits that extend to the coast.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2518 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

The uninhabited Whakaari/White Island is the 2 x 2.4 km emergent summit of a 16 x 18 km submarine volcano in the Bay of Plenty about 50 km offshore of North Island. The island consists of two overlapping andesitic-to-dacitic stratovolcanoes.
Type: Stratovolcano(es); Elevation: 294 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
The massive, dominantly rhyolitic Okataina Volcanic Centre (OVC) is surrounded by extensive ignimbrite and pyroclastic sheets produced during multiple caldera-forming eruptions.
Type: Lava dome(s); Elevation: 1111 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)

Taupo, the most active rhyolitic volcano of the Taupo volcanic zone, is a large, roughly 35-km-wide caldera with poorly defined margins. It is a type example of an "inverse volcano" that slopes inward towards the most recent vent location.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 760 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Tongariro is a large volcanic massif, located immediately NE of Ruapehu volcano, that is composed of more than a dozen composite cones constructed over a period of 275,000 years.
Type: Stratovolcano(es); Elevation: 1978 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Southern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

The submarine Clark stratovolcano lies near the southern end of the Southern Kermadec arc. This basaltic and dacitic edifice consists of a basal substrate of massive lava flows, pillow lavas, and pillow tubes overlain by volcaniclastic sediments. Craters are present along the complex crest.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -860 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Southern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Tangaroa submarine volcano in the southern Kermadec arc rises to within 600 m of the ocean surface. The volcano is elongated in a NW-SE direction and contains smaller cones on its SE to eastern flanks. A larger edifice lies further to the SE.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -600 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Ruapehu, one of New Zealand's most active volcanoes, is a complex stratovolcano constructed during at least four cone-building episodes dating to about 200,000 years ago.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 2797 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Continental crust (> 25 km)
Southern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Rumble V was discovered in 1992 at the southernmost end of the Rumble seamounts on the southern Kermadec Ridge, 17 km ESE of Rumble IV. Andesitic and basaltic andesite rocks have been dredged from this volcano, which rises more than 2,000 m to nearly 400 m below the ocean surface and shows a pristine morphology.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -400 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Southern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

The submarine Rumble IV volcano was thought to have been active from April to December 1966, based on hydrophone signals (Kibblewhite, 1967), but later evidence indicated that the hydrophone array had been damaged and the signals originated from Rumble III (Hall, 1985).
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -500 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Southern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Rumble III seamount, the largest of the Rumbles group of submarine volcanoes along the South Kermadec Ridge, rises 2,300 m from the seafloor to within about 200 m of the surface. Collapse of the edifice produced a scarp open to the west and a large debris-avalanche deposit.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -220 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Southern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Rumble II West, about 12 km NW of Rumble II East, rises 1,800 m from the ocean floor to within 1,200 m of the surface. Bathymetry shows a 2.5-3 km summit caldera about 200 m deep with a central cone. There is evidence of hydrothermal activity, and cones are present on the flanks.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -1200 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Southern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Healy submarine volcano lies along the South Kermadec Ridge and consists of an elongated edifice with a 3 x 4 km wide caldera at the NE end whose rim reaches to 1,150 m below sea level. A smaller caldera lies to the SW, and a cone, Cotton volcano, rises to 980 below sea level at the SW end of the 15-km-long complex.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -980 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Southern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

The submarine Brothers volcano, located NE of the Healy submarine volcano, contains an oval-shaped summit caldera 3-3.5 km elongated NW-SE. The high point of the dominantly dacitic edifice lies on the NW caldera rim at about 1,350 m below the ocean surface.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: -1350 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Middle Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Two volcanic cones, initially known informally as Volcano W and later named Wright, were discovered during a New Zealand-American submarine vent mapping expedition to the Kermadec arc in 2004. The deep-water basaltic volcanoes, 156 km SW of Curtis Island, both have summits cut by small calderas.
Type: Stratovolcano(es); Elevation: -900 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Middle Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Curtis and nearby Cheeseman Islands are the emergent portions of a submarine volcano along the Kermadec Ridge. The age of the small islands are considered to be Pleistocene, and rocks consist dominantly, if not entirely, of andesitic pyroclastic-flow deposits (Lloyd, 1992).
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 47 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Middle Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Macauley Island is a rim remnant of a large submarine caldera centered 8 km to the NW. The 2-km-diameter island consists of a low, gently sloping surface of rhyolitic pumice from the caldera-forming eruption truncated by steep cliffs formed of underlying basaltic lava flows.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 238 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Middle Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Giggenbach, named after volcano gas geochemist Werner Giggenbach, is a basaltic-to-dacitic submarine volcano about 30 km NW of Macauley volcano. The flat summit reaches to within 65 m of the ocean surface, has a 700-m-wide crater containing a central cone, and is cut by numerous small explosion pits and craters.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -65 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Northern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Anvil-shaped Raoul Island is the largest and northernmost of the Kermadec Islands. During the past several thousand years volcanism has been dominated by dacitic explosive eruptions. Two Holocene calderas exist, the older of which cuts the center the island and is about 2.5 x 3.5 km wide.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 516 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Northern Kermadec Volcanic Arc, New Zealand

Monowai, also known as Orion seamount, is a basaltic stratovolcano that rises from a depth of about 1,500 to within 100 m of the ocean surface about halfway between the Kermadec and Tonga island groups, at the southern end of the Tonga Ridge.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -132 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

A large submarine volcano in the Northern Kermadec Arc, ~120 km N of Monowai, is known informally as Volcano 19 from a research cruise designation. The basaltic to basaltic andesite edifice contains a 2.5 x 3.5 km outer caldera and a 1.9-km-wide inner caldera on the west.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -385 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

A large submarine volcano rises to within 65 m of the ocean surface west of Tongatapu Island. The volcano was informally named Volcano 1 by scientists on the bathymetric survey that mapped it in 2003.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -65 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

During a submarine eruption in 1907 pyroclastic material was ejected to 100 m above the ocean surface, and pumice rafts were produced. The eruption was located (on Admiralty Chart 2421) ~48 km SW of Tongatapu Island.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -68 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

An unnamed submarine volcano is located along the Tofua Volcanic Arc 35 km NW of the Niu Aunofo lighthouse on Tongatapu Island. The first documented eruptions took place in 1911 and 1923; an ephemeral island was formed in 1999. A submarine eruption in January 2017 produced discolored water visible in satellite imagery.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -296 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The small andesitic islands of Hunga Tonga and Hunga Ha'apai are part of the western and northern remnants of the rim (~6 km diameter) of a largely submarine caldera located about 30 km SSE of Falcon Island.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 114 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The ephemeral Fonuafo'ou island in the central part of the Tonga Islands is also known as Falcon Island, named after the British vessel H.M.S. Falcon, which reported a shoal in 1865. Islands up to 6 km long were formed in 1885 and 1927 eruptions; in 1933 the island had a height of more than 145 m.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -17 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The symmetrical Kao rises steeply from the ocean about 6 km N of Tofua Island in Tonga. It is elongated NNE-SSW and, with the exception of a small flat area on the SSW coast, rises at angles exceeding 35° to the summit, which has a series of small coalescing craters.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 1009 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The low, forested Tofua Island in the central part of the Tonga Islands group is the emergent summit of a large stratovolcano that was seen in eruption by Captain Cook in 1774. The summit contains a 5-km-wide caldera whose walls drop steeply about 500 m.
Type: Caldera; Elevation: 515 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

Lateiki, previously known as Metis Shoal, is a submarine volcano midway between the islands of Kao and Late that has produced a series of ephemeral islands since the first confirmed activity in the mid-19th century. An island, perhaps not in eruption, was reported in 1781 and subsequently eroded away.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 43 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Home Reef, a submarine volcano midway between Metis Shoal and Late Island in the central Tonga islands, was first reported active in the mid-19th century, when an ephemeral island formed.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -10 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

A submarine volcano along the Tofua Volcanic Arc ~45 km NW of Vava'u Island was first observed in September 2001, ~35 km S of Fonualei and 60 km NE of Late volcano. The site of the eruption is at a bathymetric depth of ~300 m.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: -40 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The 6-km-wide circular island of Late, along the Tofua volcanic arc about 55 km WSW of Vavau, contains a 400-m-wide, 150-m-deep summit crater with an ephemeral lake. The largely submerged basaltic andesite to andesitic volcano rises 1,500 m from the sea floor, with its conical summit reaching 540 m above sea level.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 540 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The small 1.2 x 2.8 km island of Tafahi is a conical stratovolcano about 7 km N of the island of Niuatoputapu in the northern Tonga Islands. It is the northernmost subaerial volcano of the Tofua volcanic arc. The basaltic andesite volcano is elongated N-S, and the summit is located on the SW side of the island.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 546 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

A submarine volcano south of Curacoa Reef at the northern end of the Tofua volcanic arc was first observed in eruption in 1973. Explosive eruptions, which produced large rafts of dacitic pumice, covering an area of more than 100 km2, were observed from the island of Tafahi, 27 km SSW.
Type: Complex; Elevation: -33 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The small island of Fonualei (~2 km diameter) contains a fumarolically active crater breached to the SE with a fresh lava flow extending to the sea and forming a rugged shoreline. Steep, inward-facing scarps mark the rim of a partially exposed caldera.
Type: Stratovolcano; Elevation: 188 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Northeast Lau Basin Volcano Group, Tonga

Niuafo'ou ("Tin Can Island") is a low 8-km-wide island that forms the summit of a largely submerged basaltic shield volcano in the north central Lau Basin about 170 km W of the northern end of the Tofua volcanic arc.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 260 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Northeast Lau Basin Volcano Group, Tonga

Two submarine volcanoes, Tafu and Maka, lie along a NE-SW-trending ridge segment in the southern part of the NE Lau Spreading Center (NELSC). The NELSC is a back-arc spreading center in the northeast part of the Lau Basin.
Type: Fissure vent; Elevation: -1400 m; Setting: Rift zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Northeast Lau Basin Volcano Group, Tonga

West Mata, a submarine volcano rising to within 1,174 m of the ocean surface, is located in the northeastern Lau Basin at the northern end of the Tofua arc, about 200 km SW of Samoa and north of the Curacoa submarine volcano.
Type: Fissure vent(s); Elevation: -1174 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Samoan Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

Vailulu`u, a massive basaltic seamount discovered in 1975, rises 4,200 m from the sea floor to a depth of 590 m. Located about one-third of the way between Ta`u and Rose islands at the E end of the American Samoas, it is considered to mark the current location of the Samoan hotspot.
Type: Shield; Elevation: -592 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Samoan Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

The 10-km-wide Ta`u Island, located at the E end of the Samoan islands, is ringed by sea cliffs. It is the emergent portion of the large Lata shield volcano. A major flank collapse event around 22 ka resulted in the steep scarps on the southern side of the island.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 931 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Samoan Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

The two triangle-shaped islands of Ofu and Olosega in eastern Samoa, with a combined length of 6 km, are separated by a narrow strait. The islands are formed by two eroded, coalescing basaltic shield volcanoes whose slopes dip to the east and west.
Type: Shield(s); Elevation: 639 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)
Samoan Hotspot Volcano Group, United States
The elongated, extensively eroded Tutuila Island in the center of the Samoan Islands consists of five Pliocene-to-Pleistocene volcanoes constructed along two or three rifts trending SSW-NNE.
Type: Tuff cone(s); Elevation: 653 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

The massive, basaltic shield volcano forming 75-km-long Upolu Island in Samoa is elongated in an E-W direction and was constructed during two periods of extensive eruptions during the Pliocene and Pleistocene.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1100 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

Savai`i, the largest and highest of the Samoan islands, consists of a massive basaltic shield volcano constructed along a WNW-ESE-trending rift zone that splits into two rifts on the east side of the 75-km-long, oval-shaped island.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1858 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Oceanic crust (< 15 km)

Taveuni, the third largest of the Fiji islands, is known as the "Garden Island" due to its rich volcanic soils. The massive, elongated basaltic shield volcano includes approximately 150 volcanic cones along a NE-SW rift that extends the length of the 40-km-long island.
Type: Shield; Elevation: 1241 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Crustal thickness unknown

The andesitic-to-dacitic Nabukelevu lava-dome complex occupies the SW end of Kadavu Island at the S end of the Fiji archipelago. The high point of the complex is Mt. Washington, an andesitic lava dome. Flat-lying dacitic lava flows are found at Cape Washington along the W coast and at Talaulia Bay on the NE coast.
Type: Lava dome(s); Elevation: 791 m; Setting: Subduction zone / Crustal thickness unknown
Bismarck Sea Volcanic Province, Papua New Guinea

The St. Andrew Strait volcano, located in the Admiralty Islands north of Papua New Guinea, consists of a series of overlapping Quaternary cones formed by rhyolitic lava flows and pyroclastic materials on Lou and Tuluman Islands. Volcanism is aligned on a curved arc extending through the 12-km-long Lou Island.
